constructs.label: Mail::to()->send()
constructs.note: A mailable is a class: the build compiles it (the dump takes the app's Mail classes, the class compiler emits the class and the kernel's Mailable base carries Laravel's fluent surface) and the mailer sends the payload Laravel sends - the recipients, the subject and the rendered view (the mailable's data goes into the view). The byte-for-byte proof is the shadow: the PHP oracle captures Laravel's MessageSent event (the from/to/cc/bcc/replyTo/subject/html/text) and the harness compares those fields with the kernel mailer's outbox - all 8 fields are identical, the log line is not compared. The four methods the edge refuses on purpose (raw, html, queue, later) fail loud at BUILD time and at request time from ONE source (ADAPTER_REFUSED, kernel/service-adapters.mjs): raw/html build the message themselves (the edge sends a compiled mailable or a payload) and queue/later need a queue consumer the Worker does not have.

constructs.label: Mail::send() (a view name)
constructs.reason: a view name is not a payload at the edge
constructs.note: Laravel's Mailer::send() has two shapes: a Mailable INSTANCE (it is sent as it is) and a VIEW NAME (Laravel renders the view with the data and sends THAT - the route answers 200 and the mail goes out). The edge has only the first shape: the compiled mailer carries a payload (a compiled Mailable, or an object with to/subject/html), so a view name throws at request time ("mail(): the message is not a payload") and the route answers 500 - the build refuses the view shape instead of shipping a route that 500s where Laravel sends the mail. A mailable still compiles (Mail::send(new OrderMail()) and Mail::to($user)->send(new OrderMail())); a dynamic first argument is NOT refused (it can hold a mailable and the build cannot prove which it is - refusing it would refuse a legal send).

constructs.label: Queue::push()
constructs.reason: the job would never run at the edge
constructs.note: The FACADE is what stays refused here: Queue::push() takes a class-name string the edge cannot resolve to a compiled class, so nothing would consume the row - Job::dispatch() on a compiled job class is the supported form (M63). Without a consumer the job would never run at the edge: the worker has no queue handler, so nothing consumes the queue binding, and the binding carries a JSON body, not a PHP job. The paths that work: a Cloudflare Queues binding with a consumer you write (a limited version is on the Workers free plan; the paid plan charges per operation), or a D1 table the cron trigger reads (a compiled job class writes the row through Job::dispatch() - M63 - or a port handler does). In Laravel the job is queued (or run inline by the sync driver) and the route answers 200.

constructs.label: Job::dispatch() on a compiled job class
constructs.note: A job class the build compiles (app/Jobs): dispatch() writes a row into the D1 lw_jobs table and the CRON TRIGGER drains it, so the job runs after the response (Laravel's database driver). The build refuses the push when the worker has no cron trigger - the job would never run - and it also refuses a push whose job class did NOT compile: the drain builds its handler map from the compiled classes, so a job the class compiler refused has no handle() for the drain and the row would be dropped unseen. Laravel's own job traits (Dispatchable, Queueable, InteractsWithQueue, SerializesModels) are allowed - their members are answered at the call site or are PHP-serializer-only - but a body that CALLS one of their members ($this->release(3)) is refused. The Queue FACADE (Queue::push) stays refused: it takes a class-name string the edge cannot resolve to a compiled class.

constructs.label: A mimes/mimetypes rule on an upload
constructs.note: PHP compares what finfo sniffs; the edge reads the image HEADER instead (kernel/image.mjs) and answers with the same guessExtension() map Symfony uses - so mimes:jpg,png,webp (and mimetypes:image/jpeg,...) answer Laravel's verdict, including the jpg/jpeg merge: guessExtension() answers jpg for image/jpeg and the vendor adds BOTH names, so mimes:jpeg ACCEPTS a real JPEG (ValidatesAttributes::validateMimes() :1764-1766). A parameter naming any other content (pdf, svg, docx, bmp) still fails loud (LW002): that verdict would be a guess.

constructs.label: A mimes rule naming a format the edge cannot sniff
constructs.reason: it reads the file's *content* type through finfo
constructs.note: mimes compiles only for the formats the header read can name (jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp, avif, heic, heif): a parameter naming any other content (pdf, svg, docx, bmp) stops the build (LW002) and NAMES the parameter, because the verdict PHP reaches comes from finfo.

constructs.label: An image/dimensions rule on an upload
constructs.note: image and dimensions are getimagesize(), a HEADER read (ValidatesAttributes::validateImage/validateDimensions): the edge reads the same header (kernel/image.mjs) and applies the same named checks, so the verdict is Laravel's. A mimes/mimetypes parameter naming a format that read cannot sniff stays refused, like any other finfo rule.

constructs.label: A rule object (Rule::file()->max())
constructs.reason: a rule object
constructs.note: A rule object in a CONTROLLER's validate() call is a class: the compiler cannot evaluate it at build time (the rules live in the controller's source), so the rule would be silently ignored and the validation would differ. constructs.label: A rule object in a FormRequest
constructs.note: The FormRequest dump reads the rules Laravel itself builds and NORMALIZES a rule object to its string form (Laravel hands the validator the object and the validator reads that string): Rule::in(['a','b']) becomes in:"a","b" - which the kernel parses exactly like Laravel (M61a). A CONDITIONAL rule object is refused (the row below).

constructs.label: A conditional rule object in a FormRequest
constructs.note: A conditional rule object (Rule::requiredIf(true), Rule::when(...)) is refused: its string form is the CONDITION evaluated at build time (RequiredIf::__toString() returns 'required' or ''), so the edge would bake the build-time branch into the rule - a request Laravel accepts could be rejected (or the other way round). The dump stops with that reason (LW003).

constructs.label: prepareForValidation() (overridden)
constructs.note: The hook is COMPILED: the build compiles the FormRequest class (the dump registers it), the compiled handler runs the hook BEFORE the validation (Laravel's order - ValidatesWhenResolvedTrait::validateResolved), and the input the hook prepares is what the rules see. The compiled class extends the kernel's kernel/form-request.mjs - the request surface the hook uses (merge(), input(), all()).

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides after() / validationData() / passedValidation()
constructs.note: All three hooks run in the compiled lifecycle, in Laravel's order: validationData() is the data source, after() registers its RETURN VALUE as a validator callback, and passedValidation() runs after the rules pass. Proven by the shadow (POST /hooked-request-demo 422/422 for the after() refusal and 200/200 carrying the passedValidation marker). The hook parameter needs its TYPE HINT (Validator $validator, and the same on the callbacks the hook registers through $validator->after(...)): an untyped parameter is LW002 (the class compiler cannot infer the validator), and the route that injects the class is then STOPPED with that reason instead of shipping a handler that answers 500 (audit #891). after() returns a single callable in the proven shape.

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides withValidator()
constructs.note: Laravel calls the hook with the validator right after it is built (Foundation/Http/FormRequest.php:110), so the app's custom messages and its after() callbacks run. The compiled class carries the hook and the lifecycle calls it with the kernel's validator, in Laravel's order. Proven by the shadow (POST /hooked-request-demo 422/422 byte-identical when withValidator() refuses the flag) and by the compiled handler's hooks: [...] list. The hook parameter needs its TYPE HINT (Validator $validator, and the same on the callbacks the hook registers through $validator->after(...)): an untyped parameter is LW002 (the class compiler cannot infer the validator), and the route that injects the class is then STOPPED with that reason instead of shipping a handler that answers 500 (audit #891). after() returns a single callable in the proven shape.
